Actor Ranya Rao Fined Rs 89.91 Crore in 113 Kg Gold Smuggling Case

Kannada actor Ranya Rao has been issued a substantial penalty of Rs 89.91 crore by the Customs Department, stemming from an alleged gold-smuggling operation. This financial imposition is part of a detailed 399-page Customs adjudication order concerning the alleged smuggling of over 113 kg of gold from Dubai to India.

Three other individuals implicated in the case—Tarun Konduru Raju, Sahil Jain, and Bharat Kumar Jain—have also faced penalties of Rs 49.51 crore, Rs 53.06 crore, and Rs 53.06 crore respectively, bringing the combined penalties against the four accused to more than Rs 244 crore.

The case gained prominence after Ranya Rao was intercepted at Bengaluru’s Kempegowda International Airport on March 3, 2025, upon arrival from Dubai. Directorate of Revenue Intelligence officials recovered 14.213 kg of foreign-origin gold, valued at approximately Rs 12.56 crore, allegedly concealed on her person. A subsequent search at her Bengaluru residence uncovered Rs 2.67 crore in cash and gold jewellery worth around Rs 2.06 crore. The investigation expanded to cover alleged gold imports between March 2024 and February 2025, and while the accused contested aspects of the probe, Customs rejected their objections.

What to watch: Ongoing criminal and other investigations related to the alleged smuggling operation.

India's Drug Panel Seeks Tighter Watch on Narcotic Medicines, States' Aid Against Fakes

India's Drugs Consultative Committee (DCC), at its 70th meeting on September 18, recommended a tighter system for tracking medicines containing narcotic and psychotropic substances. This initiative aims to curb the diversion of legally sold strong painkillers and sedatives into the illegal market, a concern outlined in the “Vision Document on Drug Control 2026 to 2029.”

The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has been tasked to address regulatory gaps by March 2027. The expert panel stressed the need for a reliable national database covering manufacture, sale, stocking, inspections, and enforcement actions. States and union territories are expected to submit monthly reports detailing licenses issued, medicine handling, inspections conducted, and actions taken, with CDSCO finalizing the reporting format.

Additionally, the committee proposed a common digital platform for data submission and analysis, suggesting the adaptation of an existing Central Bureau of Narcotics portal for end-to-end tracking of these drugs from factory to shop. All these recommendations require approval from the Drug Controller General of India (DCGI) to take effect.

Separately, the DCC is pushing to combat fake medicines, following recommendations from the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC)'s open house on February 25. States and union territories will be circulated the NHRC recommendations for comments and details on current measures, paving the way for a combined proposal from CDSCO and coordinated action among various agencies.

What to watch: The DCGI's approval and implementation timeline for the proposed drug tracking system.

Bombay HC Rules WhatsApp Video Circulation Under SC/ST Act

The Bombay High Court has ruled that circulating a video of a person belonging to the Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribe (SC/ST) community on WhatsApp falls within “public view” and attracts provisions of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. Justice Yanshivraj Khobragade delivered this ruling while dismissing a bail plea.

The appellant, Nikhil Thepale, is accused of demanding favours from a victim from the SC/ST community. When the victim refused, Thepale recorded videos and photographs of her, subsequently sending them on WhatsApp to her husband, sister-in-law, and other relatives.

Thepale faces charges under Sections 77 and 78 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Sections 66(E) and 67 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, and Sections 3(1)(r) and 3(1)(w)(ii) of the Atrocities Act. The FIR was lodged on November 5, 2025, and Thepale has been absconding since that date, a factor Justice Khobragade cited in denying bail.

What to watch: The ruling clarifies legal implications for digital content sharing involving SC/ST individuals.

Parliamentary Panel Postpones Supreme Court Visit on Simultaneous Polls Legislation

A parliamentary panel examining Bills on simultaneous polls has postponed its proposed October 6 visit to the Supreme Court for an interaction with judges. Committee chairman P.P. Chaudhary announced the decision on Thursday, October 1, 2026, citing concerns raised by Opposition leaders over the separation of powers. Mr. Chaudhary also stated that the visit was put off due to conflicting dates among committee members and his own commitments.

The proposed visit had drawn significant objections, with at least one joint committee member writing to Mr. Chaudhary to request its cancellation. The member argued that discussing the constitutional validity or merits of proposed legislation with sitting judges could raise concerns about the institutional independence of Parliament and the judiciary, creating an avoidable overlap.

Independent Rajya Sabha member Kapil Sibal publicly echoed these objections, labeling the visit "unconstitutional." Mr. Sibal, a senior advocate, highlighted that he had no precedent for a parliamentary panel interacting with Supreme Court judges on legislation potentially subject to future adjudication. He noted a committee program listed a "local study visit" to the Supreme Court on October 6, including informal discussions with the Chief Justice of India and other judges.

The joint committee is currently examining the Constitution (One Hundred and Twenty-Ninth Amendment) Bill, 2024, and the Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2024. These Bills, introduced in Lok Sabha in December 2024, aim to establish a framework for simultaneous elections to Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies.

What to watch: Future scheduling of the panel's interaction and continued debate on judicial-legislative separation.

Name Missing From SIR? If Tribunals Take A Decade To Decide Appeals, What Happens To Your Right To Vote

Delays in the judicial process, specifically concerning the resolution of appeals related to the Special Identification Register (SIR), are raising significant constitutional concerns. Advocate Jatin Bhardwaj has highlighted that if tribunals take an extensive period, potentially a decade, to decide these appeals, it could have profound implications for a citizen's fundamental right to vote.

Such prolonged delays directly impinge upon a voter’s constitutional entitlements, as articulated under Articles 14 and 21 of the Indian Constitution. Article 14 ensures equality before the law and equal protection of the laws, while Article 21 guarantees the protection of life and personal liberty. The right to vote, a cornerstone of democratic participation, is intrinsically linked to these fundamental rights.

Bhardwaj's observations underscore a critical issue within the legal framework, suggesting that the efficiency of the appellate process is vital for safeguarding democratic principles. When an individual’s name is missing from the SIR and their appeal for inclusion faces a decade-long wait, their ability to exercise their franchise is effectively suspended for an unacceptably long duration. This situation necessitates a closer examination of judicial timelines and their impact on civic rights.

What to watch: The debate surrounding judicial delays and their impact on fundamental voting rights.
